title: We beat Amazon to the patent office by four days. Here is what that actually means.
summary: Read We beat Amazon to the patent office by four days. Here is what that actually means. and explore insights on autonomous delivery, innovation, and Arrive AI updates.
body_markdown:
***TL;DR***


*Arrive AI has 10 US patents, 21 international patents, nearly 200 patent claims, and 35 years of total lifecycle built through successive filings. There are three patents most people have never heard about. And international licensing could become a meaningful revenue stream.*


In late 2014, Dan O'Toole walked into a patent attorney's office with an idea. The attorney listened to the whole thing, thought about it, and said what he says to most clients at that early stage.


"That's an interesting idea."


Dan left. John Ritchison went back to his desk and started searching. He was looking for prior art, anything that resembled what Dan had described. A smart, secure endpoint for receiving packages from drones and robots. Something that would make the handoff between an autonomous vehicle and a recipient work without anyone needing to be there.


He found nothing like it.


He picked up the phone and called Dan before Dan had even made it home.


"This is really something. There's nothing out there like this. It's probably a chance to have something totally new. A new field. We're going to make history."


That phone call is where Arrive AI's IP story starts. And interesting became exciting.


# What they filed, and who they beat


From that first conversation, Dan and John moved fast. They filed. And then they kept filing.


As it turned out, they were not alone in seeing the opportunity. Amazon was working on it. UPS was working on it. FedEx was working on it. Several companies that would eventually become competitors were working on it.


Arrive AI beat Amazon to the patent office by four to five days. They beat UPS. They beat FedEx. They beat all of them.


That is not a marketing line. It is a legal fact recorded in the patent filing record.


Arrive AI has filed continuously since late 2014, with 10 US patents granted and 18 to 19 applications currently pending.


# What the portfolio looks like today


Ten years later, here is what that early start has compounded into.


10 US patents granted. 21 international patents granted. Nearly 200 patent claims. Another 18 to 19 patents in the pipeline right now. And the most recently filed application, which John and Dan call the Aha, was just completed.


The total patent lifecycle is now approximately 35 years. That number sounds surprising until John explains how it works. A single patent has a 20-year lifespan. But every time you improve on the original idea and file a new patent, you extend the clock. Arrive AI has done that repeatedly, stacking improvements on top of improvements, and the result is a protection window that runs well past the life of any single filing.


# Three patents most people do not know about


The Arrive Point itself is the center of the IP portfolio. But John and Dan talked through three patents in this episode that get less attention and deserve more.


The Aha mechanism allows a robot to transfer a package into a sealed Arrive Point without a person present.


## The Aha


Most robots today can carry a package up to a door. What they cannot always do is transfer it into a secure receptacle without a person helping. The Aha is a patented mechanism that solves that problem. It allows a robot to bring a package to an Arrive Point, transfer it in automatically, retract, and move on. No person required.


This matters because not every robot coming off a factory floor today is built to interface directly with an Arrive Point. The Aha bridges that gap. It also works as a standalone product, which means it has potential value beyond the Arrive AI network.


## The winch patent


Most drones lower packages using a winch. Arrive AI owns a patent on doing it better. The patent covers a mechanism that locks the package in and brings it down with significantly more precision and control than the alternatives. It was acquired as part of a portfolio pickup and John calls it a good bonus. Dan calls it a hidden gem. Either way, it is relevant to a large portion of what drone delivery companies are doing right now.


## RFID multi-compartment technology


Imagine an Arrive Point deployed in a commercial building, a retirement community, or a residential complex. Multiple people, multiple packages, multiple delivery companies all using the same unit. The RFID patent covers a system that tracks individual packages across a shared, multi-compartment Arrive Point. It knows what package is coming, who it is for, when it arrived, and when it was picked up. The Arrive Point can sense an approaching recipient and open the right compartment automatically, with no action required from the person picking up.


UPS, FedEx, Amazon, Walmart, DoorDash. John says practically any carrier could use this.


# The international opportunity


Arrive AI holds granted international patents covering the UK, Europe, India, Japan, Australia, and the Gulf.


The US portfolio is the foundation. But John says the international side may be the bigger near-term opportunity.


India is ready. Japan is ready. Australia is ready. Arrive AI just received its first European Union patent approval, adding to existing UK coverage. Dubai and Saudi Arabia are active markets.


The model John describes is licensing. Companies in these countries are willing to take the Arrive AI patents, pay for the right to use them, and build out the network in their own markets. It does not require Arrive AI to deploy hardware in every country. It requires capital, local partners, and people on the ground. The portfolio is large enough now to support meaningful licensing conversations across multiple markets.


John has been saying this for a while. The patents are there. The markets are ready. It is a matter of when, not if.
